A hybrid trajectory follows a smooth ODE in each mode, changes mode at an oriented guard crossing, and applies a reset. This page defines admissible dense-output and guard-enclosure data: explicitly justified $C^1$ dense and error bounds are general inputs, and the finite rational residual-tube checker is one sufficient provider. Interval root isolation examines the whole accepted step. It returns no enabled event only after every root is excluded or proved to cross strictly opposite to its declared orientation. Failed enclosures, unresolved roots, and ambiguous event order return `inconclusive`; exhausted budgets return `budget-exhausted`; and a failed reset-domain check returns `domain-failure`, each with the certified prefix.

Under a uniform transverse-crossing bound, a guard residual and dense trajectory error give an explicit event-time error. A local reset estimate and finite induction propagate that error through finitely many separated events. The saltation formula records the first-order sensitivity across a transverse reset; it assumes differentiable mode flows, differentiable guards and resets, and a nonzero crossing derivative.

Grazing, ambiguous simultaneous events, sliding, and Zeno accumulation are outside the finite isolated-event error theorem.

rows.body: These examples calculate a transverse bouncing-ball impact and its reset error, exhibit square-root guard-root location sensitivity at a grazing contact, and compare the continuations produced by two explicit priority orders for simultaneous guards. An inelastic ball has infinitely many impacts in finite time, so the finite-event hypothesis cannot be dropped. Finally, a guard with two roots between equal-sign step endpoints shows why endpoint sign screening cannot certify that no enabled event occurred.

This page separates ideal independent fair bits from deterministic finite-state
streams. It proves that disjoint fair-bit subsequences give independent
uniforms, then quantifies midpoint discretization, including the fact that its
total-variation distance from a continuous uniform law is maximal. Finite
state and LCG results explain why a long period or uniform single-state
marginals do not imply independence. Inverse CDF, rational rejection, and
Box–Muller are developed with explicit endpoint, tail, and finite-work
behavior. The exact Box–Muller map has a product Gaussian law; its finite-bit
implementation requires certified elementary-function evaluators, and any
failed certification returns inconclusive.

The finite-bit implementation reuses the interval page's finite real evaluator
and the computed-transform page's certified unit-circle phase routine. Its
distribution-error theorem requires one fixed configuration to certify every
possible bit input, with uniform error bounds; conditioning on a successful
random sample does not establish that theorem.

This page develops finite dyadic endpoint formats and directed rounding before
defining real intervals, complex rectangles, and midpoint-radius balls. Real
interval and complex-rectangle arithmetic applies its displayed endpoint
formulas and rounds the endpoints outward. Ball operations use conservative
modulus bounds and round their output radii outward. Division across zero,
branch-cut ambiguity, overflow, and exhausted budgets return explicit
non-finite statuses.

Elementary exponential, logarithm, arctangent, trigonometric, square-root, and
complex exponential/logarithm evaluations use local range reductions and
explicit series or bisection remainders. A topological induction proves sound
range propagation through finite expression DAGs. The page also proves a
centered Taylor-model enclosure from a derivative interval and distinguishes a
certified width result from an inconclusive finite-budget output.

Natural interval evaluation preserves inclusion while it can overestimate
when a shared input appears more than once. The B page gives the subtraction
dependency, division-at-zero, and near-periodic sine cases.


The earlier finite-precision direct-factorization page is retained as reading
context. This page's item proofs use their displayed local directed-rounding,
root, interval and series suppliers; they consume no NA-02 factorization,
solve bound or round-to-nearest success model. Its retained page requirement
does not turn that unrelated model into a mathematical premise here.

This page extends the canonical finite Fourier transform and radix-two FFT with computed error bounds, arbitrary-length reductions, trigonometric transforms, and convolution. Its radix-two stability estimate assumes round-to-nearest, normal-range successful operations, and a certified error bound for every twiddle. The product-stage constant is explicit: $\eta=10u+\epsilon_{\rm tw}$; the $O(u\log N)$ shorthand requires $\epsilon_{\rm tw}=O(u)$ and $u\log N$ small. A phase-evaluation budget that cannot certify its requested enclosure returns inconclusive. The interval evaluator's arctangent definition is shown to use the same canonical $\pi$ as the Fourier and chirp formulas.

Mixed-radix Cooley–Tukey and Bluestein supply exact arbitrary-length reductions. Bluestein pads to a supported power of two $M\ge2N-1$ and records chirp-phase error separately from the FFT-convolution error. Arithmetic counts exclude integer factor search, interval phase evaluation, memory traffic, and bit complexity; no general mixed-radix stability theorem is asserted here.

DCT-II uses the even extension and the stated endpoint normalization; DST-I uses the odd extension and its fixed endpoint zeros. Both inverses are proved directly, and the DCT-II recovers Chebyshev coefficients at first-kind roots. Linear convolution uses zero padding to prevent circular aliasing. Its error bound separates forward transforms, pointwise products, inverse transform, and final scaling, conditional on successful operations.

rows.body:
Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature is defined by integrating the Chebyshev–Lobatto
interpolant, with explicit DCT-I endpoint conventions and a midpoint case at
degree zero. It is exact through degree $n$. For $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$ and
$g(t)=f(m+dt)$, the approximation estimate is
$$\left|\int_a^b f-Q_{n,[a,b]}(f)\right|\le (b-a)(1+\Lambda_n^L)E_n(g),$$
where $E_n(g)$ is the best uniform degree-$n$ error on $[-1,1]$ and
$\Lambda_n^L$ is the Lobatto interpolation norm. Affine pullback identifies
$E_n(g)$ with the best degree-$n$ error of $f$ on $[a,b]$. The factor
$(b-a)$ follows by integrating the interpolation residual over the physical
interval; on $[-1,1]$ the factor is $2$. The source contract's shorter
$[-1,1]$ expression without that factor is not used.

The page also defines a finite nested Romberg table. A finite Euler–Maclaurin
formula supplies a uniform even-power expansion, and a separate induction
proves the cancellations under that expansion hypothesis. An observed error
ratio alone does not establish the hypothesis or the resulting order.

For a finite quadrature functional annihilating polynomials through degree
$r-1$, the Peano kernel gives an integral remainder and an $L^1$ bound. The
nine-node closed Newton–Cotes rule is verified exactly through degree nine;
its negative weights give a sample-perturbation norm larger than its signed
weight sum. The even-extension DFT algorithm inherits only the computed-DFT
status in its supplier contract and makes no new stability or accuracy claim.

rows.body:
This page treats two distinct finite-dimensional contact models. For a fixed nonempty compact convex set, it defines the outward normal-cone evolution and explicit projection Euler, proves the normal-cone and projection facts used by the method, and proves uniqueness under the choice assumptions inherited through its absolutely-continuous FTC supplier. Countable Choice is used for almost-everywhere differentiability, Lebesgue differentiation, and null-set unions; Dependent Choice is inherited through the integrated FTC identities. The exact Euler interpolants converge uniformly; with certified per-step projection residuals, the error is bounded by a constant times $\sqrt h$ plus the accumulated projection tolerances. The computation reports an unresolved status when a projection certificate cannot be produced within its budget.

For one-dimensional unilateral impact, the first-impact algorithm accepts constant acceleration and a prescribed restitution coefficient. It returns free flight when the complete incoming-root list is empty and the gap is certified nonnegative on the whole step, including a grazing zero that does not cause penetration; it returns `unresolved` when root completeness or nonpenetration cannot be certified. Its proof establishes momentum balance, complementarity, and the kinetic-energy change at the instantaneous impact; it does not continue through sustained contact or repeated impacts. A separate frictionless binary-sphere law is proved by direct impulse algebra. The event-driven sphere algorithm accepts explicitly valid finite dense/event providers and consumes the event page's general time-error, reset-error and mode-flow interfaces. Its certificates enforce nonpenetrating reference states and account for every guard zero; any unlisted or nontransverse zero returns `unresolved`. A local geometry lemma supplies the full-state guard/normal and reset Lipschitz bounds. Event-bracket width, guard residual, prior reset error and outgoing flow during a reporting lag are kept separate; only matched smooth prefixes and aligned reset states are compared. This retains arbitrary C1 force fields without claiming a generic provider construction from a rational-expression checker. Frictional multi-contact, simultaneous impacts, grazing event times, Zeno behavior, and a penalty-to-rigid limit are outside the proved event guarantees.

## Objective

This page separates adaptive Simpson's finite procedure and its heuristic
indicator from a conditional certified mode. The $1/15$ relation follows
from a local composite Simpson asymptotic expansion and is relatively accurate
only when its leading coefficient is nonzero; it does not certify any finite
run. The capped procedure always returns an explicit accepted, cap-reached,
or failure status. A separate interval mode encloses the integral only when
sound point-value and fourth-derivative enclosure oracles are supplied; an
inconclusive enclosure never reports the requested tolerance as achieved.

## Summary

An embedded explicit Runge–Kutta pair shares stages and reports the difference between its high and low outputs. The difference estimates the lower-order local defect only asymptotically when its leading coefficient is nonzero; it is used as a heuristic by a fully specified accept/reject controller with norm scaling, safety factor, step bounds, and a finite attempt budget. Neither an accepted step nor a completed controller run certifies global error or diagnoses stiffness. The generic fixed uniform-mesh global-error theorem has a distinct mesh and exact-defect premise.

For the Euler–Heun pair, the page derives both local defects and constructs a quadratic dense output with its own uniform within-step error. It also states the continuous-residual a posteriori error estimate. A separate choice-free proof covers piecewise-$C^1$ reconstructions, and a bounded residual plus one-sided Lipschitz estimate yields the integrating-factor bound.

The validated branch is intentionally finite and narrow: it checks rational ODE expression DAGs, dyadic polynomial reconstructions, interval enclosures, residuals, Jacobian bounds, and a strict radius supersolution. Its soundness argument accounts for the actual stored reconstruction, including interpolation or stage error represented in its coefficients. Unsupported operations or failed inclusions return inconclusive; no embedded difference is treated as a residual certificate.

This page develops verified point and family linear solves, Krawczyk inclusion,
real determinant sign checks, Hermitian eigenvalue enclosures, inertia based
eigenvalue bisection, and a complex resolvent cover validator. Point residual
certificates use rounded operations with explicit error allowances; family
certificates use outward interval enclosures. Every validator reports an
inconclusive or range status when its numerical checks do not establish the
required inequalities. Failed determinant, interval pivot, or inertia checks
are not treated as evidence of singularity.

The complex Hermitian results are derived through realification where the
available Weyl and inertia interfaces are stated for real symmetric matrices.
The contour validator proves a uniform resolvent bound only on its supplied
disk cover; it does not count enclosed eigenvalues. Interval dependent claims
use the current outward-arithmetic definitions and their DAG soundness theorem;
they remain drafts pending independent review.

## Examples

These examples check an exact residual enclosure for a system with condition
number $2^{20}$, show why an interval family containing a singular member
cannot receive a uniform inverse certificate, and carry out ordered Hermitian
eigenvalue bisection with exact inertia queries. The bisection example records
the exact shifts and counts, including the finite query budget.

rows.body:
This page gives two certified root-isolation routes. Exact rational polynomials use gcd squarefree decomposition, Sturm variation at exact rational endpoints, and dyadic bisection; the coefficient-height root bound and separation estimate prove that the exact process terminates. The gcd route preserves multiplicities, so even-multiplicity roots need no sign change.

For $C^1$ functions on an open interval, scalar interval Newton uses valid function and derivative enclosures. A disjoint Newton intersection or a range enclosure excluding zero proves absence; strict inclusion in the interval interior proves existence and, when the derivative enclosure excludes zero, uniqueness. A failed test leaves the box unresolved.

For $C^1$ maps on an open convex domain, the Krawczyk operator combines a certified nonsingular point preconditioner, an interval Jacobian, and outward interval operations. Strict inclusion in the box interior proves existence by Brouwer. Uniqueness requires a separately certified contraction bound; strict inclusion alone is not a uniqueness claim. The smooth-function isolator reports certified boxes plus unresolved boxes after finite budgets and makes no all-roots claim unless the unresolved list is empty.

The nonlinear-equation, outward-interval, and verified-linear-systems interfaces are retained. The polynomial proofs also reuse the published fundamental theorem of algebra and exact polynomial gcd results. The local closed-box fixed-point reduction uses the published closed-ball Brouwer theorem; the interval Jacobian, Sturm count, multiplicity and root-separation arguments are proved locally with their explicitly listed prerequisites.

rows.body:
## Objective

This page fixes an autonomous phase by adding the unknown period and one scalar
phase condition to the periodic endpoint equations. It records the neutral
Floquet multiplier, the exact shooting Jacobian, and the equivalence between a
simple neutral multiplier plus a transverse phase and invertibility of that
bordered Jacobian. For the autonomous flow rescaled to $[0,1]$, it defines
single/multiple-shooting and midpoint-collocation residuals, proves an explicit
bounded-inverse estimate for the continuous phase-bordered BVP, and gives
explicit residual and $h^2$ midpoint-error constants on a local branch.

Candidate solvers have finite budgets and never certify a root by their
residual alone. A rational range-oracle interface encloses the flow and
variational equation with explicit Euler defects; Krawczyk strict inclusion,
its separate contraction bound, and a nonstationarity range certify a unique
phase-fixed periodic solution within a box. A left/right-conditioned finite
bound handles an isolated simple multiplier. For clusters, the page uses a
verified resolvent cover, explicit midpoint quadrature error, a rational
$\pi$ interval, and the argument principle to count multipliers with
algebraic multiplicity. Orbital stability is concluded only when the neutral
cluster count is one and every other complete cluster enclosure is strictly
inside the unit circle. A unit-circle overlap leaves the verdict inconclusive.

The C2 common-tube flow theorem proves the required shooting-map regularity from
the field hypothesis and supplies the second variation equation.
Pseudo-arclength continuation corrects the parameterized phase-bordered
residual with a validated section equation; a fold in the parameter projection
does not itself make the full branch residual singular. The AUTO manual is
used as an algorithm and notation source, not as a replacement for the local
proofs. Exact supplier interfaces and remaining cross-batch checks are listed
in the batch notes and dependency evidence.

## Objective

The examples compute a stable planar cycle whose bad phase slice makes the
shooting Jacobian singular, while a transverse phase makes it invertible. A
coarse Euler step overestimates a stable transverse mode and produces a
spurious multiplier of modulus greater than one. A near-unit interval
enclosure demonstrates why a cluster count alone cannot decide stability.
The van der Pol example states the exact conditional implication from a future
validated orbit and complete strict Floquet cluster certificate; it supplies
no fabricated numerical orbit or interval values.

rows.body:
An analytic matrix function can be defined by applying one scalar holomorphic
branch and its derivatives to the Jordan blocks. Finite Hermite interpolation
produces a polynomial representing those same jets, which proves independence
of the chosen Jordan form, similarity invariance, the contour formula, and the
normal spectral formula. The page also records the principal logarithm and
square root on the slit plane and the Fréchet derivative of the exponential.

For the exponential, the diagonal Padé approximant is fixed at a finite order.
Its scalar remainder and the recurrence for squaring defects are proved
directly. A rational contour estimate transfers scalar error to a matrix only
when a uniform resolvent bound is available; this condition matters for
nonnormal matrices. The scaling-and-squaring bound is conditional on exact
denominator and squaring audits, a validated contour resolvent bound, and
caller-supplied contour topology. The validator does not establish the contour
index or count enclosed eigenvalues. Candidate-only runs carry no error claim.

The Schur–Parlett procedure verifies exact Schur and Sylvester identities and
returns an inconclusive status when those checks or required block data fail.
Its recurrence has a separate exact correctness proof; no floating-point
stability claim is made. Newton polar and matrix-sign algorithms likewise
separate finite rounded iterations from convergence theorems about their exact
sequences.

The candidate denominator solve reuses stored reflector kernels on both the
factorization and right-hand side, defines complex pivot division through
rounded real components, and enforces its candidate-operation budget. Exact
residual and error-controller formulas use finite exact real-RAM loops; the
fully encoded rational adapter retains a finite exact rational implementation.
No decoder or bit-computability is presumed for arbitrary stored reals.

A separate result proves termination for the seven finite procedures and the instrumented candidate-operation budgets. Every rounded kernel primitive is dispatched before spending its budget; partial candidates are not squared or audited as complete. Contour bounds use coefficient-weighted chain length, while exact analytic/Newton convergence and certification hypotheses remain separate.

This page develops certified global search on compact boxes. Its spatial branch-and-bound procedure records valid lower bounds, verified feasible upper bounds, empty-box proofs, and explicit unavailable or budget-exhausted statuses. A gap certificate proves global epsilon-optimality. With exact midpoint upper bounds and lower bounds consistent on shrinking branches, the unlimited unconstrained procedure eventually reaches every positive epsilon; singleton boxes require an exact report.

Outward-rounded interval evaluation and validated Lipschitz midpoint bounds supply rigorous box enclosures. The bilinear McCormick envelope is proved to be the convex hull of the product graph, and a factorable relaxation interface admits nonlinear graph enclosures only when their domain hypotheses and coefficients are certified. A dual-feasible pair with a verified lower bound for its dual value yields a lower bound for the original problem. Bounded integer variables use deterministic median splits with finite enumeration as a fallback, and no polynomial running-time claim is made.

Constraint pruning requires a sound infeasibility bound. For finitely many continuous constraints on a nonempty compact box, a positive uniform separation margin and finite-time sound bounds consistent on shrinking boxes permit finite certified emptiness detection. The Gaussian-process section consumes the published finite posterior theorem, handles positive noise and every observed-covariance-positive-definite case, and retains acquisition maximization error. It proves only a sequential posterior update and finite-search termination, not generic regret or global optimality. The page supplies no duplicate Newton or validated root-solving algorithm.

rows.body:
For a finite positive Borel measure on a compact interval whose support has at
least $m+1$ points, the moment pairing is positive definite through degree
$m-1$ under the exactness-order moment assumptions, and through degree $m$ on
the stronger degree-$2m$ branch. The degree-$m$ monic polynomial orthogonal to
lower degrees has $m$ simple roots in the interval's interior. Integrating the corresponding
Lagrange cardinal polynomials defines the Gaussian weights; polynomial
division and orthogonality give exactness through degree $2m-1$, and applying
exactness to squared cardinal polynomials gives strict positivity.

The moment interface separates two claims. Moments through degree $2m-1$
suffice for the node construction and exactness theorem. The Hermite
mean-value remainder also needs the degree-$2m$ moment that makes
$\int p_m^2\,d\mu$ finite and positive. The proof constructs the degree-$m$
polynomial from the positive degree-$(m-1)$ moment matrix, so it does not
assume a degree-$m$ norm on the exactness-only branch.

The three-term recurrence gives a real symmetric tridiagonal Jacobi matrix.
Consecutive orthogonal polynomials, equivalently consecutive leading principal
Jacobi truncations, have strictly interlacing roots. Its eigenvalues are exactly the Gaussian nodes, and a normalized eigenvector's
first-coordinate square times the total mass is the associated weight. The
Golub–Welsch procedure uses a finite eigensolver only to propose Ritz data;
outward interval residual, Gram, and spectral checks must certify every
returned enclosure. A failed finite check returns inconclusive and makes no
error claim. Tensor products preserve coordinatewise exactness, with
$\prod_jm_j$ nodes for coordinate orders $m_j$. A separate Tonelli–Fubini
argument identifies the algebraic product-moment functional with integration
under the finite product measure, so polynomial-chaos coefficient exactness
uses a proved measure interface.
